home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Regina: EnerGuide evaluations (home energy assessments), costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book a home energy assessment (EnerGuide evaluation) in Regina: 12 licensed organizations, local prices, Saskatchewan rebates and what 70% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 12 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in Regina. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in Regina houses, and which Saskatchewan rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Regina homes
sections.html:
Of Regina's 69,170 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 70% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Regina house dates from 1971–1980, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Regina gets about 5,597 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −32.4°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Regina International. That's the 5th-highest heating demand of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the Regina area, 76% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace and about 10% with a boiler and radiators; natural gas is the main heating energy for 70% of households and electricity for 19% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

There's no provincial rebate; the City of Saskatoon quotes $500–$600 as typical for the initial EnerGuide evaluation and $300–$400 for the follow-up.

Most providers quote the initial (pre-upgrade) and follow-up (post-upgrade) visits separately. Rebate programs that pay on measured improvement need both, so ask for the combined price.

sections.h2: How a home energy assessment (EnerGuide evaluation) works
sections.html:
• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

sections.h2: Why air leakage matters in Regina
sections.html:
Regina gets about 5,597 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −32.4°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Regina International. That's the 5th-highest heating demand of the 70 cities we cover.

Of Regina's 69,170 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 70% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses usually test leakier than newer ones, and an EnerGuide report compares your result with homes of the same era, so you can see whether your house is typical or a problem.

• Combustion safety. In the Regina area, the main heating energy is natural gas for 70% of households. A tighter house changes how fuel-burning appliances vent, so the spillage check should be repeated after serious air sealing. Combustion safety testing in Regina
  • Radon. Sealing shifts the pressure balance between the house and the soil. Health Canada's 2012 survey found 25.5% of 94 homes tested in the Regina Qu'Appelle Regional Health Authority health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 46.6% (1 in 2) of houses at or above the guideline for the Regina, SK (Regina CMA) metro area. Test before and after big air-sealing jobs. A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. There's no provincial rebate; the City of Saskatoon quotes $500–$600 as typical for the initial EnerGuide evaluation and $300–$400 for the follow-up.

• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Regina: CSA F280-12 heat pump sizing for −32.4°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280-12 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Regina homes, sized to the local −32.4°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −32.4°C for Regina, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Regina International.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Regina
sections.html:
−32.4°C is the 4th-coldest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −32.4°C, even cold-climate heat pumps lose capacity just when you need heat most. The room-by-room number tells you how much the heat pump can cover and how much backup heat to plan for, rather than guessing from square footage.

In the Regina area, 76% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace and about 10% with a boiler and radiators; natural gas is the main heating energy for 70% of households and electricity for 19% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

The National Building Code 2020 requires the heating capacity for a house to be worked out with CSA F280, and its list of referenced documents names the 2012 edition, CSA F280-12. Provincial codes can name their own edition and climate values, so ask your designer which ones the calculation uses.

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

providers.heading: NRCan-licensed service organizations serving Regina
providers.note: Many energy advisors also do room-by-room CSA F280 calculations for an extra fee; HVAC designers do them too. Ask for the F280 report itself, not just an equipment recommendation.

faq.q: Is duct cleaning the same thing?
faq.a: No. Cleaning removes dust; it doesn't find or seal leaks. A leakage test measures where air is lost.

faq.q: What is ductwork pressure testing?
faq.a: The same thing as a duct leakage test: registers are sealed, a calibrated fan pressurizes the ducts, and the airflow needed to hold the test pressure shows how leaky they are.

faq.q: Should I close vents in unused rooms?
faq.a: Usually not. Closing registers raises duct pressure and can increase leakage elsewhere in the system.

ventilation-assessment.lede: Condensation on windows, musty basements and stuffy bedrooms are ventilation and humidity problems, and they're easy to confuse with insulation problems. A ventilation assessment measures which one you have.

sections.h2: Why Regina homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
Regina gets about 5,597 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −32.4°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Regina International. On Regina's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of Regina's 69,170 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 70% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (24% of Regina's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.
  • Actual airflow from bath and kitchen fans, and whether they vent outside rather than into the attic.
  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

faq.q: Will more insulation stop ice dams?

radon-testing.h1: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in Regina
radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Regina: long-term monitoring, kits and mitigation
radon-testing.description: Radon in Regina: Health Canada survey results for the Regina Qu'Appelle Regional Health Authority region (25.5% above the guideline), how to run a 91-day long-term test, digital monitors versus alpha-track kits, and mitigation by C-NRPP professionals ($2,000–$3,000).
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 25.5% of homes tested in the Regina Qu'Appelle Regional Health Authority health region were above the guideline, and only a long-term test tells you about your own house.

glance.sub: the Regina, SK (Regina CMA) metro area

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 25.5% of 94 homes tested in the Regina Qu'Appelle Regional Health Authority health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 46.6% (1 in 2) of houses at or above the guideline for the Regina, SK (Regina CMA) metro area.

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

sections.h2: Long-term monitoring: how to test properly
sections.html:
Health Canada's measurement guide asks for a long-term test with at least 91 days in the heating season, when closed windows and the stack effect make readings higher, so the result is a conservative estimate of the yearly average. It recommends testing for 3 to 12 months. Our radon testing guide walks through each step.

Place the detector on the lowest level where someone spends more than four hours a day, at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls, and at least 1 m from vents, windows and doors; avoid kitchens, laundry rooms and bathrooms. The choice of device:

  • Alpha track detectors record radon's alpha particles on a plastic film; you mail them to a lab when the test ends. A long-term kit costs about $30–$80 including the lab fee (Windsor-Essex County Health Unit).
  • Electret ion chambers lose charge as radon ionizes the air inside; a lab reads the voltage drop.
  • Digital (electronic) monitors read continuously and show results on a screen or an app, and cost more (Lung Saskatchewan sells one for $189). For a long-term test, Health Canada says to use one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing, and it still has to run at least three months.
  • Continuous monitoring after mitigation: a digital monitor left running lets you watch for changes between the follow-up long-term tests Health Canada recommends.

• Lung Saskatchewan sells long-term kits for $65 including lab analysis and supports free monitor lending at libraries including the Regina and Saskatoon public libraries.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Regina postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: If your level is high: mitigation
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends fixing levels above 200 Bq/m³ within a year, and sooner the higher the level. The usual fix is a sub-slab depressurization system (a sealed pipe through the floor and a fan venting outside), which Health Canada says costs about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour and cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Hire a professional certified for mitigation under C-NRPP. After a system goes in:

  • A C-NRPP professional runs a short test starting at least 24 hours after the fan is turned on.
  • A long-term three-month test follows in the next fall or winter, done by a company other than the installer.
  • With an active system, Health Canada recommends a long-term test within two years of activation and every five years after that, and again after renovations.
  • Check the system's pressure gauge (manometer) regularly and never switch the fan off. It costs about $50 to $75 a year to run; a replacement fan is $200 to $300.

• Since January 1, 2024, Saskatchewan's adoption of the 2020 National Building Code requires a radon rough-in in new homes.
  • Saskatchewan's Home Renovation Tax Credit is back for 2025 and later tax years, and Lung Saskatchewan lists radon mitigation as an eligible expense.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Regina?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 25.5% of 94 homes tested in the Regina Qu'Appelle Regional Health Authority health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 46.6% (1 in 2) of houses at or above the guideline for the Regina, SK (Regina CMA) metro area. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least 91 days, in the heating season. Health Canada recommends 3 to 12 months; short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Regina?
faq.a: Lung Saskatchewan sells long-term kits for $65 including lab analysis and supports free monitor lending at libraries including the Regina and Saskatoon public libraries. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits, for about $30–$80 including the lab fee.

faq.q: Digital radon monitor or alpha-track kit?
faq.a: An alpha-track kit is the cheaper long-term test: it sits for three months or more and goes to a lab. A digital monitor shows readings as it goes and can keep running after mitigation; for a long-term result, use one that has passed C-NRPP testing and run it for at least three months.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Health Canada puts a sub-slab depressurization system at about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour, plus about $50 to $75 a year to run the fan. Hire a C-NRPP-certified mitigation professional.

faq.q: Should I keep monitoring after mitigation?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test in the following heating season, another within two years of activation, and one every five years after that. A digital monitor running in between shows if anything changes.

carbon-monoxide-testing.h1: Carbon monoxide testing and CO alarms in Regina
carbon-monoxide-testing.title: Carbon monoxide testing and CO alarms in Regina: Saskatchewan detector installation rules and appliance checks
carbon-monoxide-testing.description: CO alarms and carbon monoxide testing for Regina homes: what Saskatchewan law requires, where alarms must go, why it matters with 70% of households heating with natural gas, and how appliances get checked.
carbon-monoxide-testing.lede: Carbon monoxide is odourless and can kill. Saskatchewan requires CO alarms in all residential buildings regardless of age (enforced since July 1, 2022), and from November 1, 2026, 'Henry's Law' requires one in every residential suite, including secondary suites.

sections.html: Saskatchewan requires CO alarms in all residential buildings regardless of age (enforced since July 1, 2022), and from November 1, 2026, 'Henry's Law' requires one in every residential suite, including secondary suites.

sections.h2: Where CO alarms go: installation rules in Saskatchewan
sections.html:
What the rules say about installing alarms:

  • Required in all residential buildings, whatever their age, that contain a fuel-burning appliance, an attached garage or more than one suite (enforced since July 1, 2022).
  • In a house, put an alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door, plus one in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance such as a wood stove.
  • From November 1, 2026, Henry's Law requires a CO alarm in every residential suite, including houses with secondary suites.
  • For new houses, the National Building Code 2020 (Article 9.32.3.9) requires a CO alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door when the home has a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage, an alarm in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance (on or near the ceiling unless the maker's instructions say otherwise), and interconnected alarms in a house with a secondary suite.

In the Regina area, the main heating energy is natural gas for 70% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023). Any fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage is a potential CO source.

Single-detached houses make up 63% of Regina's households; many have an attached garage, another reason to put an alarm near the door into the house.

• Alarms next to sleeping areas and on every storey, tested monthly and replaced by their end-of-life date (usually 7 to 10 years).
  • Annual service of fuel-burning appliances by a licensed technician.
  • A combustion spillage test during an energy evaluation, which catches a venting problem before it produces CO.

faq.q: Are carbon monoxide alarms mandatory in Regina?
faq.a: Saskatchewan requires CO alarms in all residential buildings regardless of age (enforced since July 1, 2022), and from November 1, 2026, 'Henry's Law' requires one in every residential suite, including secondary suites.

faq.q: Where should CO alarms go in Saskatchewan?
faq.a: Required in all residential buildings, whatever their age, that contain a fuel-burning appliance, an attached garage or more than one suite (enforced since July 1, 2022). In a house, put an alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door, plus one in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance such as a wood stove. For new houses, the National Building Code 2020 (Article 9.32.3.9) requires a CO alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door when the home has a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage, an alarm in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance (on or near the ceiling unless the maker's instructions say otherwise), and interconnected alarms in a house with a secondary suite.

faq.q: How long do CO alarms last?
faq.a: Most have an end-of-life date of 7 to 10 years printed on the unit; replace them by then even if they still beep when tested.

mold-testing.h1: Mould and indoor air quality testing in Regina
mold-testing.title: Mould and indoor air quality (IAQ) testing in Regina: air sampling, inspection and remediation
mold-testing.description: Mould inspection and indoor air quality testing in Regina: when mold sampling is worth it, why cold winters cause condensation, the CMHC and Health Canada size rules for cleanup, and when to hire a remediation contractor.
mold-testing.lede: Mould sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mould problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure. Here's how to inspect a home in Regina, when air quality testing helps, and how much cleanup you can safely do yourself.

glance.sub: or if it keeps coming back

sections.h2: Why mould shows up in Regina homes
sections.html:
Regina gets about 5,597 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −32.4°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Regina International. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mould usually starts in Regina houses.

Of Regina's 69,170 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 70% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

sections.h2: Mould inspection: when sampling is worth it
sections.html:
Start by looking and smelling: stains, discoloured patches, peeling paint and a musty odour, especially in basements, bathrooms, window frames and closets on outside walls. Health Canada says measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually unnecessary.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Air or surface sampling helps in three cases:

  • You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

sections.h2: Cleanup and remediation: the size rules
sections.html:
CMHC and Health Canada sort mould by size, and the size decides who should clean it up:

SizeWhat countsWho should clean it
SmallOne to three patches, each smaller than 1 m²A healthy homeowner, with water and unscented dish detergent (CMHC)
MediumMore than three patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m² (32 square feet)Trained help; homeowners only with training and precautions
LargeA patch larger than 3 m², or many patches through the houseA qualified mould remediation contractor (CMHC)
  • Fix the moisture source first: a leak, poor drainage, or condensation from high humidity. Health Canada recommends 30–50% relative humidity.
  • For a small cleanup, wear safety glasses or goggles, an N95 mask if possible and household rubber gloves. People at risk from mould shouldn't clean it and should stay away.
  • Health Canada suggests professional help for extensive mould, especially growth that keeps coming back after cleaning.

sections.h2: Choosing a tester, lab or remediation contractor
sections.html:
Ask any Regina tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause. For remediation, get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the area is cleaned.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Regina · Our mould and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mould testing cost in Regina?
faq.a: We found no reputable Canadian source for the cost of a professional mould assessment, so get two or three written quotes and ask how many samples are included, which lab analyzes them and what the report covers.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: How much mould can I clean myself?
faq.a: CMHC says a healthy homeowner can clean one to three patches, each under 1 m², with water and unscented dish detergent. Larger areas need trained help or a remediation contractor.

faq.q: When should I hire a mould remediation contractor?
faq.a: For a single patch over 3 m², many patches through the house, or mould that keeps coming back after cleaning (CMHC, Health Canada).

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.h1: Asbestos testing and inspection in Regina
asbestos-testing.title: Asbestos testing and inspection in Regina: vermiculite, labs, and Saskatchewan abatement and removal rules
asbestos-testing.description: Asbestos inspection and testing in Regina, where 70% of houses were built before 1991: what to sample, lab costs, the Saskatchewan rules for renovation, and what abatement and removal involve if a test is positive.
asbestos-testing.lede: About 48,600 Regina houses (70%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Regina houses
sections.html:
Of Regina's 69,170 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 70% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

Saskatchewan requires a competent person to inventory asbestos-containing materials in workplace buildings, and contractors must notify Occupational Health and Safety at least 14 days before high-risk asbestos work.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

Our asbestos and vermiculite guide · Attic inspections in Regina

sections.h2: If it's positive: abatement and removal
sections.html:
Leave the material alone until a plan is in place. For vermiculite, Health Canada says not to use the attic for storage, to keep children out and to seal gaps around the attic hatch, light fixtures and outlets, and to hire professionals trained to handle asbestos if you plan to renovate.

In Saskatchewan: Contractors must notify Occupational Health and Safety at least 14 days before high-risk asbestos work, and suspect material is treated as asbestos until it's shown to be asbestos-free.

Abatement is quoted separately from testing. Get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the waste will be disposed of.

faq.q: Do I need an asbestos test before renovating in Regina?
faq.a: If the house was built before 1991 and the work will disturb insulation, flooring, plaster or duct wrap, test first. Saskatchewan requires a competent person to inventory asbestos-containing materials in workplace buildings, and contractors must notify Occupational Health and Safety at least 14 days before high-risk asbestos work.

faq.q: How much does asbestos testing cost?
faq.a: About $50–$150 per lab sample, plus the assessor's visit. Abatement, if needed, is quoted separately.

faq.q: What should I do if I have vermiculite in the attic?
faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

faq.q: Who removes asbestos in Saskatchewan?
faq.a: Contractors must notify Occupational Health and Safety at least 14 days before high-risk asbestos work, and suspect material is treated as asbestos until it's shown to be asbestos-free.

lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in Regina: at-risk homes, testing and safe abatement
lead-paint-testing.description: 22% of Regina's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 22% of Regina's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 48% built from 1961 to 1990.

sections.h2: Which Regina homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Regina's 69,170 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 70% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

sections.h2: If it's positive: lead paint abatement
sections.html:
Health Canada says leaving lead-based paint alone is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach, and covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling adds protection. Paint that's chipping, flaking or within reach of children is a serious hazard and has to come off carefully; consider hiring an expert before you start.

No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. must include lead in pre-renovation and demolition hazard inspections, and in Yukon before demolition. If you do the work yourself, Health Canada's precautions are:

  • Don't use sanders, heat guns or blowlamps: they create toxic dust and fumes. For do-it-yourself work, Health Canada suggests a chemical paint-stripper paste applied with a brush.
  • Move furniture out or cover it with plastic, seal doorways and vents with plastic sheeting and tape, and run a fan blowing out through an open window.
  • Wear goggles, gloves and a good-quality mask, work in 10-minute stretches with breaks outdoors, and don't eat, drink or smoke in the work area.
  • Clean up daily: put scrapings in a sealed container marked Hazardous Waste, follow your municipality's disposal instructions, and wipe surfaces with a damp cloth you throw away.
  • Keep children and pregnant people away until the work is done; Health Canada says there is no known safe level of lead exposure.

faq.q: Does my Regina house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

faq.q: Should I remove lead paint or cover it?
faq.a: Health Canada says leaving it alone or covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach. Never sand it or use a heat gun, and consider hiring an expert for removal.

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Regina: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Regina: ASHRAE levels, no mandatory reporting rule, and 1 utility or government incentive for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Regina: no mandatory reporting rule and 1 incentive program we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Regina
sections.html: • No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.SK).

• Commercial Energy Optimization Program (CEOP) (SaskPower and SaskEnergy (administered by CLEAResult, with the Government of Canada)): Free consulting. Energy Support Services (small/medium businesses using under 2 GWh/yr): identify opportunities, build business cases, track projects and savings. Energy Coach Services (large, about 2 GWh+): the same plus up to $30,000 toward an energy champion. CEOP Incentive Services for upgrades: $0.13/kWh non-lighting, $0.06/kWh lighting, $15/GJ gas, up to 50% of costs and $100,000 per project per fuel. Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do Regina buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: We found no mandatory reporting rule for Regina buildings as of September 28, 2026.

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Regina?
faq.a: Yes: Commercial Energy Optimization Program (CEOP). Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
